posts.image_prompt: A narrow carved stone tunnel deep underground in soft volcanic rock, lit by flickering oil lamps, a huge round millstone-like stone door set into the wall, chambers branching off into darkness, cinematic
posts.caption:
🕳️ A MAN KNOCKED DOWN A WALL AND FOUND A CITY

In 1963, a resident of Derinkuyu in Cappadocia, Turkey, was renovating his home. When he broke through a basement wall, he found a hidden passage.

It led to an entire underground city.

Derinkuyu goes down roughly 280 feet and has at least 18 levels. Historians estimate it could shelter up to 20,000 people, along with stables, storage and even a church.

Huge stone doors could seal it from the inside. Dozens of ventilation shafts carried fresh air deep underground.

Its origins may reach back to around the 8th century BC, and it was expanded over the centuries, at least into the Byzantine era. People still used it as a refuge into the early 20th century.

Nobody knows exactly who dug the first tunnel.

Would you have lived underground to stay safe?

posts.title: The king who crashed the price of gold

scenes.image_prompt: A long royal caravan of camels and richly dressed travelers crossing golden Sahara dunes at sunrise, banners fluttering, cinematic wide shot
scenes.narration: In thirteen twenty-four, one king spent so much gold its value crashed.

scenes.image_prompt: A West African king of the fourteenth century in flowing robes and a gold crown seated on a throne in an earthen palace, attendants around him, warm light
scenes.narration: He was Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire in West Africa, a land famous for its gold.

scenes.image_prompt: A medieval Cairo street with minarets and crowded markets, a grand procession arriving, merchants watching in awe, dusty golden light
scenes.narration: On his pilgrimage to Mecca, he stopped in Cairo. The scholar al-Umari wrote that he gave loads of gold to the treasury and to court officials.

scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of a merchant's wooden table in a medieval market covered in gold nuggets and silver coins, a balance scale, candlelight
scenes.narration: Cairo's merchants profited so much that gold became cheap. Al-Umari said its value had still not recovered about twelve years later.

scenes.image_prompt: An illuminated medieval map-maker's workshop with a large painted parchment map showing a crowned king on a throne holding a golden object, no lettering
scenes.narration: His fame spread to Europe. A famous European map made in thirteen seventy-five shows him on a throne, holding a piece of gold.

scenes.image_prompt: A lone camel silhouetted on a desert ridge at sunset, warm orange sky
scenes.narration: Was he the richest person who ever lived? Tell us what you think, and follow for more.

posts.caption:
👑 One pilgrimage. So much gold that its price fell.

In 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali passed through Cairo on his way to Mecca. The scholar al-Umari recorded that gold lost value there for years afterwards.

Was he history's richest person? Weigh in 👇

posts.image_prompt: A small square ancient steatite stamp seal carved with a bull-like animal and a few small abstract symbols above it, resting on sand at a mud-brick excavation site, warm afternoon light, macro photography
posts.caption:
🔍 A GREAT CIVILIZATION WHOSE WRITING NO ONE CAN READ

The Indus Valley Civilization built planned cities in what is now Pakistan and northwest India. Its writing flourished around 2600–1900 BC.

Archaeologists have found thousands of short inscriptions, mostly on small stone stamp seals, from dozens of sites.

The problem? They are tiny. The average inscription is only about five signs long, and none found so far is longer than about 26.

There are roughly 400 different signs, and there's no agreement on what language they record. No bilingual inscription — like Egypt's Rosetta Stone — has ever been found to help.

Do you think the Indus script will ever be deciphered?

posts.title: The shipwreck that started a race for longitude
posts.hook_text: ON THIS DAY: A FLEET HIT ROCKS

scenes.image_prompt: Wooden warships of 1707 smashing onto jagged black rocks in a stormy night sea, lantern lights, crashing white surf
scenes.narration: On this night in 1707, a whole British fleet hit the rocks.

scenes.image_prompt: A fleet of 18th-century warships under full sail in fog, sailing toward a dim rocky coastline, grey dusk
scenes.narration: Admiral Sir Cloudesley Shovell was bringing his warships home to England. In the dark, they reached the Isles of Scilly.
scenes.label: SCILLY

scenes.image_prompt: Navigators in tricorn hats bent over a sea chart with dividers by lamplight, worried faces
scenes.narration: The navigators believed they were clear of land. They were wrong about where they were.

scenes.image_prompt: A massive warship splitting on a reef, masts falling, tiny lifeboat in towering waves
scenes.narration: Four ships were lost. More than thirteen hundred men died, including the admiral himself.

scenes.image_prompt: An 18th-century Parliament chamber with men in powdered wigs debating, a scroll reading a reward notice
scenes.narration: The disaster became famous. In 1714, Parliament offered up to twenty thousand pounds to anyone who could find a ship's longitude at sea.

scenes.image_prompt: A beautifully crafted brass and wood marine clock with intricate gears on a velvet table, soft workshop light
scenes.narration: A clockmaker named John Harrison spent decades building sea clocks to solve it.
scenes.label: JOHN HARRISON

scenes.image_prompt: Old nautical charts with faded coastlines spread on a table, a brass compass and candle on top
scenes.narration: The twist? Historians now doubt longitude alone was to blame. Poor charts, currents and bad compasses may have mattered just as much.

scenes.image_prompt: Calm sea at dawn over the jagged Western Rocks of Scilly, gulls, no ships
scenes.narration: Human error or impossible conditions? Tell us. Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🌊 ON THIS DAY in 1707, a British fleet sailed straight onto the rocks of the Isles of Scilly.

Admiral Sir Cloudesley Shovell's navigators thought they were safely clear of land. Four ships were lost and well over a thousand men died, the admiral among them.

The disaster helped push Parliament to pass the Longitude Act of 1714, offering up to £20,000 for a reliable way to find longitude at sea — the challenge clockmaker John Harrison spent his life on.

But historians now argue over the cause: longitude, bad charts, currents or compasses. Which do you think sank the fleet? 👇

posts.image_headline: The first leap from the sky
posts.caption:
📅 ON THIS DAY in 1797, a man cut the only rope holding him to a balloon — 3,000 feet above Paris.

On October 22, 1797, André-Jacques Garnerin rose over Parc Monceau in Paris, sitting in a basket beneath a silk parachute that was tied to a balloon by a rope.

At about 1,000 metres up, he cut the rope.

The balloon shot away. Garnerin dropped. His canopy, about 23 feet across, had no hole at the top to let air escape, so the basket swung back and forth violently all the way down.

He landed unhurt — and made history with one of the first successful parachute descents.

Two years later, his student and future wife, Jeanne Geneviève Labrosse, became the first woman to make a parachute descent. In 1802 Garnerin made the first parachute descent in England.

The fix for the wild swinging, a vent at the top of the canopy, was suggested by astronomer Jérôme Lalande in 1804. Many parachutes still have one today.

Would you have cut that rope?

posts.title: Trapped in the Ice: How Shackleton Brought All 28 Men Home from Antarctica
posts.hook_text: THEIR SHIP SANK. NOBODY KNEW THEY WERE ALIVE.

scenes.narration: On November 21, 1915, in the frozen Weddell Sea, 28 men watched their ship slip beneath the ice. They were hundreds of miles from help, and no one knew where they were.
scenes.label: 21 NOV 1915

scenes.narration: Their leader was Ernest Shackleton. Their ship was the Endurance. What happened next became one of the greatest survival stories ever told.
Stay to the end for an 800-mile voyage in an open lifeboat, a desperate 36-hour march across the mountains of South Georgia, and the discovery of the lost wreck in 2022.
The Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition left Plymouth on August 8, 1914. Its goal was to make the first crossing of Antarctica on foot.
scenes.label: 8 AUG 1914

scenes.narration: By November, Endurance had reached the whaling stations of South Georgia, the last outpost before the ice. Then she sailed south.
scenes.label: SOUTH GEORGIA

scenes.narration: In January 1915, the pack ice closed around her. By January 24 she was frozen in, unable to move in any direction.
scenes.label: JAN 1915

scenes.narration: Her captain and navigator was Frank Worsley. His careful position records would matter more than anyone could have imagined, more than a century later.
For months, the ship drifted with the ice. The crew lived aboard through the long polar winter, while the pressure on her hull slowly built.
On October 27, 1915, Shackleton gave the order to abandon ship. The men moved onto the ice with their lifeboats, their sled dogs and whatever supplies they could carry from the ship.
scenes.label: 27 OCT 1915

scenes.narration: Photographer Frank Hurley filmed the bow being crushed and the masts collapsing. His pictures are why we can still see it today.
On November 21, a pressure wave lifted the stern, and dropped her. Endurance was gone.
The men lived first at Ocean Camp, then at Patience Camp, on floating ice that was slowly drifting north. They held on there for more than three months.
scenes.label: PATIENCE CAMP

scenes.narration: In April 1916, the ice began to break up. They climbed into three lifeboats and set out across freezing open water.
scenes.label: APR 1916

scenes.narration: They reached Elephant Island, an uninhabited, storm-battered rock. There they built a shelter by turning two of the boats upside down. Twenty-two of them would wait there.
scenes.label: ELEPHANT ISLAND

scenes.narration: Elephant Island was far from any shipping route. So on April 24, 1916, Shackleton and five men set off in the third boat, the James Caird, to fetch help.
scenes.label: 24 APR 1916

scenes.narration: Shackleton, Worsley, Tom Crean, Harry McNish, John Vincent and Timothy McCarthy sailed about 800 miles across the Southern Ocean towards South Georgia.
scenes.label: 800 MILES

scenes.narration: It was a small open boat on one of the roughest oceans on Earth, and Worsley had to find a single island. On May 10, after sixteen days at sea, they landed at King Haakon Bay.
scenes.label: 10 MAY 1916

scenes.narration: But they had landed on the far side of the island. The whaling station at Stromness, and help, lay on the other side of its mountains.
Shackleton, Worsley and Crean crossed those mountains in about 36 hours, and walked into the whaling station at Stromness.
scenes.label: 36 HOURS

scenes.narration: Getting back to Elephant Island took several failed attempts. Finally, on August 30, 1916, the Chilean ship Yelcho, under Luis Pardo, reached the island.
scenes.label: 30 AUG 1916

scenes.narration: Every one of the men left behind was still alive. Of the 28 who sailed on Endurance, not one was lost.
There was tragedy elsewhere: on the other side of Antarctica, three men of the expedition's Ross Sea party died.
Then, on March 5, 2022, the Endurance22 expedition found the wreck, 3,008 metres down, about four nautical miles from Worsley's recorded position.
scenes.label: 5 MAR 2022

scenes.narration: She was standing upright in remarkable condition, her wheel intact, and the name Endurance still clear on her stern.
Was it Shackleton's leadership, Worsley's navigation, or plain luck that saved them? Tell us what you think. Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🧊 Their ship sank in the Antarctic ice. Nobody in the world knew they were alive.

In 1915, Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance was trapped and crushed in the Weddell Sea, leaving 28 men stranded on drifting ice.

This documentary follows them from the ice camps to Elephant Island, through an 800-mile voyage in an open lifeboat and a 36-hour crossing of South Georgia's mountains — and to the moment the wreck was found, 3,008 metres down, in 2022.

What do you think saved them: leadership, navigation, or luck?
